getStarted.title: Get started on NHCX
getStarted.lede: Four stages take any participant from registration to production. What you build inside them depends on which half of a claim you handle, so say which you are and the stages fill in.
getStarted.question: Which side of a claim are you on?

roles.label: Provider
roles.note: A hospital, clinic, nursing home or day care centre, or the HMIS or TMS vendor building for one. You raise claims.

steps.title: Register on the ABDM sandbox
steps.text: Fill in the sandbox registration form to get your credentials and participant code. The exchange addresses you by that code, so one integration reaches every payer on it.

steps.title: Send what your system already holds
steps.text: The diagnosis, procedure, bill lines and codes your HMIS already records become one signed FHIR bundle. Nothing is re-keyed and nothing is scanned.

steps.title: Build the raising half of the flow
steps.text: Check coverage eligibility, raise the pre-auth, submit the claim, and read the payment notice that comes back. Each one is a request you send and a callback you handle.

steps.title: Certify, then apply for production
steps.text: Complete the functional and security test cases for the provider role in the sandbox, then submit both certificates. NHCX assigns your production role and credentials.

roles.label: Payer
roles.note: An insurer, TPA, state health agency or government scheme such as PM-JAY. You adjudicate claims.

steps.title: Register on the ABDM sandbox
steps.text: Fill in the sandbox registration form to get your credentials and participant code. Providers reach you by that code, so one integration serves all of them.

steps.title: Make your rules readable to the exchange
steps.text: Plans, package rates and the checks you apply become rules a request can be matched against, so a clean claim is decided without anyone opening an attachment.

steps.title: Build the answering half of the flow
steps.text: Receive eligibility checks, pre-auth requests and claims, respond on each, and send the payment notice. Each one is a request you handle and a callback you send.

steps.title: Certify, then apply for production
steps.text: Complete the functional and security test cases for the payer role in the sandbox, then submit both certificates. NHCX assigns your production role and credentials.

both: You build against NHCX once and reach every counterparty on it, instead of integrating with each payer or hospital in turn.
The sandbox is free and open before you apply for anything, so you can read the specification by building against it.
Certification is per role. A vendor building for both sides certifies for both.

hero.text: NHCX puts India’s health claims on one interoperable standard, so provider and payer systems exchange claim data directly.

journey.eyebrow: How a typical flow looks like
journey.title: From the hospital’s HMIS to a decision, and back again

steps.title: Structured at source
steps.text: The discharge summary, bill lines and codes leave the HMIS as a signed FHIR R4 bundle. No PDFs, no re-typing.

steps.title: Schema-checked and signed
steps.text: Validated against the specification and signed on both sides, leaving an immutable trail.

steps.title: Route and deliver
steps.text: The exchange identifies the payer and delivers the claim. One integration, every payer.

steps.title: Auto-adjudicated
steps.text: Policy active, member verified. Package rate matched. Duplicate and abuse checks clear.

steps.title: Back to the provider
steps.text: The decision travels the same path in reverse and lands in the HMIS: a round trip, not a one-way pipe.

steps.title: Register on the ABDM sandbox
steps.text: Fill in the sandbox registration form and you can start building. ABHA verification is not required in the sandbox: you only need it for production, where beneficiaries are authenticated for real.

steps.title: Integrate and test the APIs
steps.text: Build against the HCX sandbox: coverage eligibility, pre-auth, claim, payment notice and communication, each with its on_ callback. Use the Postman collections and the DevTools console to exercise every flow.

steps.title: Get sandbox certification
steps.text: Complete the functional and security test cases for your role. The affiliate sandbox may ask for additional security review (STQC or CERT-In) before it issues the certificates.

steps.title: Apply for production
steps.text: Share the functional and security certificates. NHCX assigns your role in production, provisions credentials and registers you as a participant, then you go live.

understand.title: A national exchange for health-claim data, run by the National Health Authority under ABDM
understand.intro: The National Health Claims Exchange is the digital gateway between the people who deliver care and the people who pay for it. A hospital submits a claim once, as coded FHIR data; the exchange checks and signs it, finds the payer, and delivers it. The decision comes back the same way. It began as the Health Claims Platform (HCP) and was renamed NHCX on the industry’s suggestion; its specifications were developed in the open with insurers, TPAs and state health agencies.

meta.title: PM-JAY on NHCX
meta.description: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY gives eligible families cashless treatment at empanelled hospitals. NHCX is the exchange those claims can travel on: one standard message from hospital to payer and back.

hero.lede: Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana gives eligible families cashless secondary and tertiary treatment at empanelled hospitals. NHCX is the rail those claims travel on: one standard message, one set of rules, and a claim raised in the hospital’s own HMIS instead of re-keyed into a separate portal.

items.title: Cover a family can use
items.text: Up to ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, with no premium to pay at the point of care.

items.title: Cashless at the hospital
items.text: An eligible patient is treated and discharged without paying the hospital; the claim is settled between the hospital and the scheme afterwards.

items.title: Run by NHA with the states
items.text: The National Health Authority runs PM-JAY nationally, and each State Health Agency runs it in its own state, with its own empanelment and its own claim processing.

changed.title: Three things a hospital does differently
changed.lede: The scheme is the same and so is the cover. What changes is where the claim is raised, how the patient is proved to be the beneficiary, and what happens to a claim that arrives clean.

items.was: Re-keyed into a separate claims portal
items.text: The claim is composed in the software the hospital already runs, from the diagnosis, procedure and bill lines it already holds. No second data entry, no staff switching systems to submit what has just been recorded.
The patient is authenticated against their Ayushman record at the hospital, so who was treated is settled at the point of care rather than queried weeks later against a paper trail.

A claim that arrives coded, complete and validated can be priced against the scheme’s rules as it lands, so the straightforward majority settle first and human review is spent on the cases that need it.

journey.text: The same four moves every claim makes, with the standards doing the work in between. Nothing here is particular to one hospital’s software or one state’s claim system.

steps.title: The hospital raises the claim
steps.text: The treating hospital composes the claim from what it already recorded (diagnosis, procedure, drugs, bill lines) as one structured FHIR bundle rather than a folder of scans.

steps.title: NHCX carries it
steps.text: The exchange routes the bundle to the right payer for that patient and that state, signed and encrypted, and hands back a receipt the hospital can quote later.

steps.title: The payer decides
steps.text: The State Health Agency or its insurer reads a machine-readable claim, so routine cases can be priced by rules and only the ones that need a human get one.

steps.title: The answer comes home
steps.text: Approval, query or rejection returns on the same rail against the same claim id, so the hospital knows where every claim stands without a phone call.

items: One integration, not one per payer: the same bundle format serves PM-JAY, state schemes and private insurers.
Claims validated before they leave, so incomplete ones are caught at the desk instead of coming back as queries weeks later.
A readable trail for every claim, which is what a disputed settlement actually turns on.

groups.who: For State Health Agencies and insurers
items: Coded clinical data instead of scanned paper, so adjudication rules can run on the claim as it arrives.
The same message shape from every empanelled hospital, whatever software that hospital runs.
Faster, more traceable settlement, and fewer cycles spent asking hospitals for what was already sent.

start.title: Connecting a PM-JAY hospital or payer
start.lede: Integration is the same for a scheme claim as for any other: read the specification, build a bundle that validates, rehearse the whole flow against the sandbox, then apply for the environment you need.

hero.intro: Two tools and no third thing to choose between: one that teaches and rehearses the exchange in a browser tab, one that carries it in production.

consoleCard.title: DevTools
consoleCard.copy: The exchange end to end, in a tab: read how an endpoint behaves, build a bundle that validates, and trade claims with a mock payer until every flow passes. Nothing you do here touches your servers.

adapterCard.title: NHCX Adapter
adapterCard.copy: The piece you actually deploy. Post a FHIR bundle to it, read a plain callback back, and it does the headers, the encryption, the certificates and the acknowledgements in between. One JSON config, no database.

useCases.title: Starting from zero
useCases.text: Fourteen chapters across two tracks, from what the exchange is to how a claim settles, each ending in a short check that remembers where you got to.

useCases.title: Preparing your first claim
useCases.text: Compose eligibility, pre-authorisation, claim and payment bundles against the ABDM profiles, and find what is wrong before a real send does.

useCases.title: Testing with no counterparty
useCases.text: A mock payer answers, so a whole flow runs end to end before anyone assigns you a partner. When one fails, the decrypted request and callback are both there.

adapter.title: NHCX Adapter
introParts: One binary between your system and NHCX. Your software posts a FHIR bundle to it and reads a plain callback back; the adapter does the
headers, the encryption, the certificates and the acknowledgements. Nothing else about your system changes.
adapter.useCasesTitle: What you’d use the adapter for

useCases.title: Put an existing system on NHCX
useCases.text: Your HMIS or claims software posts a bundle to one local endpoint and reads plain JSON back. Nothing inside it learns the protocol, and one adapter can carry several participant codes.

useCases.title: Move from sandbox to production
useCases.text: One switch in config.json. The same calls and the same endpoints, pointed at the other environment’s registry and credentials.

useCases.title: Settle a disputed claim
useCases.text: Pull the exact request and callback for a correlation id months later, decrypted and readable, and replay it if the payer asks.

meta.title: NHCX is one prompt away · AI skill
meta.description: An agent skill that teaches your coding assistant the National Health Claim Exchange: the protocol, the FHIR bundles, the envelope and the sandbox, so an integration can be asked for rather than assembled by hand.

hero.lede: An agent skill that teaches the coding assistant you already use what the exchange actually is: its endpoints and callbacks, the FHIR bundle behind each flow, the envelope that carries it, and a sandbox to try the whole thing against. You describe the claim. It writes the integration and proves it.

transcripts.prompt: Send a pre-authorisation for a cataract day-care admission to the sandbox.
steps: read the pre-authorisation cycle: request, acknowledgement, callback
composed the bundle: Claim, Coverage, Patient, Organization
validated against the ABDM profiles, no errors
posted to the sandbox and waited for the callback
transcripts.reply: The mock payer approved it in 4.2 seconds. The request, the callback and the decrypted payload are written to nhcx/preauth-01/ so you can read what actually went over the wire.

transcripts.prompt: This claim came back rejected. Tell me what to fix.
steps: decrypted the callback and read the error block
matched the code against the error catalogue
traced it to one bill line with no coded product
patched the bundle and revalidated it
transcripts.reply: The envelope was fine; the payer rejected the content. One item carried a description but no code, so it could not be priced. It is coded now and the bundle validates, ready to resend.

transcripts.prompt: Wire our hospital system to NHCX and prove it end to end.
steps: generated the adapter configuration from your endpoints
checked the certificates and the participant code
ran eligibility, pre-authorisation, claim and payment notice
all four flows settled against the mock payer
transcripts.reply: Four flows pass. Your system keeps posting plain JSON to one local endpoint; the encryption, the protocol headers and the acknowledgements all happen inside the adapter.

transcripts.prompt: What changes when we move this integration to production?
steps: listed every value that differs from the sandbox
diffed your configuration against the production shape
flagged two secrets still sitting in the repository
wrote the cutover as a checklist
transcripts.reply: Nine values change and two of them are secrets that should never have been committed. The checklist is in MOVE-TO-PRODUCTION.md, each line pointing at the part of the specification behind it.

loop.titleLead: It reads before it writes, and
loop.text: An answer you cannot check is worth little on a network that settles money. The skill works in a loop: study the rule, build the request, test it against the ABDM profiles, run it against the sandbox, and go round again until the flow passes or it can tell you exactly why it will not.

phases.title: Study
phases.text: It pulls the part of the specification the task needs: the flow, the endpoints it uses, the profile each bundle has to satisfy. Nothing is answered from memory.

phases.title: Build
phases.text: It writes the request in your project, in the language and the shape already there, instead of pasting a sample that assumes somebody else’s stack.

phases.title: Test
phases.text: The bundle goes against the ABDM profiles and the envelope against the protocol at your desk, so a malformed claim is caught before it is anyone else’s problem.

phases.title: Run
phases.text: It sends to the sandbox, waits for the asynchronous callback, decrypts it and reads it. A failure is the next input rather than the end of the attempt.

knows.titleAccent: The exchange, in a form an agent can act on
ledeParts: The NHCX specification, compiled into instructions an assistant follows rather than pages a person reads.

cards.title: The exchange itself
cards.text: Which call starts a flow, which acknowledgement comes back on the same connection, and which answer arrives later on your callback endpoint. The asynchronous shape of NHCX is the part integrations get wrong first.

cards.title: The bundle behind each flow
cards.text: Eligibility, pre-authorisation, claim and payment notice, each as the FHIR resources the ABDM profiles require, with the fields that must be coded rather than typed.

cards.title: Signing and encryption
cards.text: How a payload is encrypted for one recipient, what the protocol headers carry, and which key the other participant will use to open it.

cards.title: What a rejection means
cards.text: The error codes and their real causes, so a returned claim reads as an instruction (this field, this value, this fix) instead of a wall.

cards.title: Where to try it
cards.text: How sandbox access is granted, what the mock payer will answer, and every value that changes on the day you point the same code at production.

cards.title: The adapter you deploy
cards.text: The one binary that sits between a hospital system and the exchange: its configuration, the endpoints it exposes inward, and how to run it beside software you are not allowed to rewrite.

prompts.text: Copy one into the assistant in your editor. Each of these ends in something you can run, not in a paragraph explaining what you could run.
items: Set up NHCX in this repository: sandbox config, a callback endpoint, and one eligibility check that passes.
Build a pre-authorisation bundle for a cataract day-care admission and validate it against the ABDM profiles.
This callback came back rejected. Decrypt it, tell me which field is wrong, and fix the bundle.
Add the NHCX adapter beside our existing hospital system without changing how the HIS posts a claim.
List everything that changes when we move this integration from the sandbox to production.

rules.text: An agent with credentials on a national network needs a shorter leash than one writing a landing page. These are the four it is held to.

items.title: Sandbox until you say otherwise
items.text: The skill points at the sandbox. Production is a thing you ask for in words, not a default it can wander into.

items.title: Your machine, your data
items.text: It works in your repository with your credentials. Nothing about a patient goes anywhere except to the exchange you addressed it to.

items.title: Every rule comes with its source
items.text: A field is required because a named section of the specification says so, and the answer says which section. You can check it without trusting it.

items.title: It stops rather than invents
items.text: Where the specification is silent or the sandbox disagrees with it, the skill says so and hands the decision back, instead of filling the gap with a plausible field name.

close.lede: The skill is a folder of instructions and specifications in your project. Any assistant that reads skills from the repository picks it up; nothing else about your setup changes.
noteParts: You still need credentials to send anything: the skill writes and validates without them, and the sandbox answers once your application is through.
